Therefore, if the existing insulation is below R-6, the old wrap is removed and replaced with high-performance R- 12 insulation. Ducts integrated with the building envelope are not modified. For applicable dwelling units, where duct insulation in unconditioned spaces is currently below the IECC requirement, we also assume that ducts integrated with the building envelope assembly fall below code—specifically, less than R-8 in climate zones 1–4 and less than R-12 in climate zones 5–8. Based on these assumptions, this measure assumes = the average duct insulation level across the entire dwelling unit reaches an R-value of R-8 after improvements. Duct leakage can be defined as a percentage of airflow or as an airflow leakage volume value. The percentage rating is calculated by comparing the duct system’s measured leakage rate to the air handler’s flow rate. This metric is useful for assessing HVAC system efficiency. The leakage volume value is measured in cubic feet per minute (cfm) airflow leakage per 100 ft2 of conditioned floor area. It estimates the total air volume leaked from the system, helping to visualize the extent of leakage and estimate the scope of repair work needed. The IECC (2012) limits leakage to 4 cfm per 100 ft2 of conditioned floor area when the air handler is installed and 3 cfm when it is not installed. Industry standards generally require new duct systems to be sealed to 6% or less leakage, while altered or existing systems may be allowed a leakage rate of up to 15% (Eco Performance Builders, 2025). Therefore, this measure will not seal ducts with a leakage rate of 6% or less. After improving ductwork, the target for duct leakage after a retrofit is recommended to be 5% (Andrews, 2001). However, many contractors strive for even lower leakage levels. For example, Eco Performance Builders (2025), a retrofit company based in the Bay Area, reports an average duct leakage of under 1% after a retrofit, while PV Heating, Cooling & Plumbing (Peavey, 2025), based in the Atlanta metropolitan area, aims for 4% leakage or less. To reach this target, PV Heating, Cooling & Plumbing technicians seal all duct connections and joints using only duct mastic and high-quality mastic tape. Once a duct leakage test confirms that leakage is below the target threshold, they proceed to insulate the sealed duct areas. Achieving 4% duct leakage requires significant effort. In a typical home, it often takes multiple cycles of sealing and testing to meet this performance standard.
